newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: French government at odds over EMU remarks.
newsitem.headline: French government at odds over EMU remarks.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government was at odds over Europe's planned single currency on Tuesday after Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's spokesman disowned comments by his junior minister for Europe.

European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici sparked doubts about economic and monetary union for the second time in a week by saying in a radio interview that Paris would decide whether or not to join the euro after assessing public finances.
He told Radio Luxembourg the next six months would be crucial for the future of the single currency.
"We must assess the state of our public finances, and it will be in light of this situation that we will decide whether or not to move to the euro," Moscovici said.
After hours of uncertainty, Jospin's spokesman Manuel Valls told reporters in Amsterdam, where both men were attending a European Union summit, that Moscovici had spoken out of turn.
"He spoke too quickly. This is not an expression either of our political will or of a strategy," Valls said.

He said the position spelled out several times by Jospin was that France would meet the criteria and deadline set to launch EMU in January 1999. "This will not be done to the detriment of employment and growth," he added.

The prime minister is due to deliver his government's keynote policy statement to parliament on Thursday and is expected to announce an audit of public finances to check how far France really is from the EMU target of limiting the overall deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.

The previous centre-right government defeated on June 1 had insisted that France was on target to meet the criterion, but Socialist officials have said the first indications they have received on tax revenues and welfare accounts suggest otherwise.
Valls said there was no deliberate policy of saying one thing at home and another to France's European partners.

Asked whether Moscovici had not been merely repeating what the Socialists had said during last month's election campaign, he said: "The campaign was one thing and being a minister afterwards is something different."
It was the second time in a week that Moscovici had appeared to step out of line on economic and monetary union.
Last Tuesday, he said he did not expect the government would approve a controversial budget deficit-limiting EU stability pact at this week's Amsterdam summit.

Hours later, President Jacques Chirac made clear he wanted to reach a deal in Amsterdam, and Jospin indicated he would try to do so. The agreement was sealed on Monday after France's EU partners accepted a statement pledging greater efforts to boost growth and employment.
